tldr: RoboColiseum is an integrated platform featuring high-precision system identification that achieves a 0.9686 task-score correlation between real robots and simulation, a flexible runtime decoupling physics and rendering, and eight evaluation tracks designed to uncover the true physical capabilities of state-of-the-art VLA models and LLM agents.
hero_caption: Correlation of task scores between real and simulated environments. Across 4 robot configurations and 16 tasks (22 configurations in total), it achieves an exceptionally high agreement with a Pearson correlation of 0.9686 (R² = 0.938), confirming that evaluations in simulation accurately mirror real-world robot behavior.
overview:
Research on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and LLM-powered robot agents is moving fast. However, testing them safely and fairly in the physical world is both costly and time-consuming. Simulators are the obvious alternative, but traditional simulation evaluation faces a serious hurdle: policies that succeed in simulation often fail on real hardware (the Sim2Real gap). Furthermore, there has been no unified benchmark spanning both rigid bodies and deformables like cloth and paper, let alone covering everything from single-arm manipulation to whole-body coordination and fine precision.

To bridge this gap, the authors created RoboColiseum, a platform designed for the co-evolution of simulation, evaluation, and models. First, by replaying recorded real-world commands, the platform tightly identifies dynamic parameters for both the robot and objects (system identification), aligning simulated behaviors with the real world. Next, it establishes a shared protocol that decouples physics engines (PhysX, Newton, libuipc) from rendering backends (Isaac Sim, OVRTX), enabling seamless coupling between deformable simulation (IPC) and articulated dynamics (MuJoCo).

Building on this foundation, the authors designed an eight-track benchmark. It covers fundamental capabilities like instruction following and spatial reasoning (Season I), as well as four advanced dimensions: dexterous manipulation, whole-body coordination, precision manipulation, and cross-embodiment transfer (Season II). Across 22 paired real-simulation setups, they demonstrated a 0.9686 task score correlation. When evaluating leading VLA models and agent systems under identical criteria, the benchmark clearly exposed their critical shortcomings in precision tasks and multi-fingered dexterous control.
contributions: Demonstrated an exceptionally high Pearson correlation of 0.9686 in task scores across 22 paired real–simulation configurations using a recorded-command replay approach.

Introduced the 'RoboColiseum Protocol' to decouple physics from rendering, enabling flexible task creation involving both rigid and deformable bodies (cloth, paper, soft bodies) in contact-rich settings.

Formulated eight evaluation tracks spanning instruction following, robustness, dexterous manipulation, whole-body coordination, precision manipulation, and cross-embodiment transfer, alongside a budget-aware progress scoring metric.

Evaluated three recent VLA models and eight LLM-based agent systems side by side on a public leaderboard, systematically revealing performance boundaries, strengths, and weaknesses, particularly in precision and multi-fingered manipulation.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need the Co-Evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models?
sections.summary: With the rise of VLAs and world action models, we need environments that evaluate models seamlessly from instruction understanding to physical execution. This paper introduces RoboColiseum, an integrated foundation addressing three core challenges: physical parameter validity, coupled deformable simulation, and the separation of reasoning from execution resources.
sections.details:
With advances in Embodied AI, VLA models that convert vision and language directly into low-level robot actions, as well as policies based on world models, are attracting immense attention. Because evaluating them repeatably in real physical setups is extremely challenging, researchers rely heavily on simulators. However, conventional simulation evaluation faces three major hurdles.

First is 'Sim2Real reliability.' Even if parameters are identified to be physically plausible, that does not guarantee they translate into real-world task success rates. We must verify whether task scores match when pairing real robots with simulation.

Second is 'representing composite physical phenomena.' The contact and deformation of flexible objects like cloth, paper, and sponges require numerical treatments fundamentally different from rigid robot links. A flexible simulation architecture capable of coupling them efficiently is essential.

Third is 'decoupling reasoning, execution, and resource consumption.' To tell whether a model is genuinely capable or merely brute-forcing attempts, strict evaluation metrics must set budgets on action steps and inference calls.

RoboColiseum tackles these issues directly through three pillars: accurate behavior replication via system identification and command replay, a decoupled protocol separating physics from rendering, and a comprehensive eight-track benchmark.

sections.heading: Matching Behavior Beyond Appearance: Rigorous System Identification and Real2Sim
sections.summary: By replaying recorded joint control commands directly in simulation, the framework identifies robot dynamics and object contact parameters. It validates not just position tracking but torque errors and contact state formation step by step, ensuring genuine physical fidelity rather than superficial visual resemblance.
sections.details:
When tuning a simulator, the most important goal is not making things 'look similar,' but ensuring that 'identical commands yield identical motion and contact.' This work builds a systematic Real2Sim pipeline that independently identifies robot dynamics, object contact parameters, and controller/sensor configurations.

### II-A Real2Sim Formulation and Replay Protocol
A sequence of joint and gripper targets $u_k$ captured on the real robot is faithfully replayed at roughly 100 Hz, with the physics engine advancing in 1 ms substeps. Crucially, it does not rely on artificial grasp attachments (magnetic suction); all grasping and manipulation rely purely on contact friction. As a result, the task cannot be reproduced unless both the robot tracking and the contact models are accurate.

### II-B Robot and Object System Identification
For robot arms (such as the G2 crsB), friction, damping, armature inertia, and rigid link inertia parameters are not solved all at once. Instead, they are isolated and estimated through staged excitation experiments. Constant-velocity sweeps first isolate friction and damping, sinusoidal motions then capture acceleration-dependent terms, and coupled Fourier motions identify link inertia matrices. This sequence prevents overfitting caused by friction and inertia canceling each other out. For object identification, masses are fixed while optimizing to minimize gripper-aperture RMSE (root mean square error) during grasp, alongside visual keypoint residuals.

### II-C Controller Alignment and Validation Hierarchy
If simulator PD gains ($K_p = 1000\mathbf{I}_7$, along with axis-specific $K_d$ settings) are too stiff, joint positions may track well even when the underlying physics model is wrong—a phenomenon known as masking. To detect this, the authors independently evaluate both joint position errors and sensor torque RMSE. Furthermore, in object identification, grasping can fail even when pixel residuals decrease; residual checks and task success verification are therefore kept separate.

captions.F2: Workflow of object replay and identification using recorded commands. Two paths are evaluated: parameter transfer (top), where parameters fitted in MuJoCo are ported to other engines, and native adaptation (bottom), where configurations are tuned directly in the engine's native environment to check task success and observation errors.
captions.F4: Replication RMSE heatmaps across joints of a 7-DoF arm. The left panel shows joint angle error (deg), and the right panel shows sensor torque error (N·m), evaluated across three excitation patterns: Fourier motion, constant-velocity sweep, and sinusoidal motion.
captions.F3: Trajectory and visual residual diagnostics for shuttlecock (top) and whiteboard marker (bottom) handover tasks in PhysX. They illustrate how tracking shifts relative to real-world observations (black dots) before and after parameter identification, highlighting that lower pixel residuals alone do not guarantee grasp success.

sections.heading: From Rigid Bodies to Cloth and Paper: Pluggable Decoupled Architecture
sections.summary: The authors created a shared protocol that loosely couples physics, rendering, and task control. Rigid-body dynamics and deformable calculations (IPC) are distributed across different engines, coupling robot motions with material deformations both efficiently and accurately.
sections.details:
Some robotics tasks run fine with fast rigid-body simulation, while others—like cloth folding—require advanced finite element methods. Handling all of these inside a single closed engine is impractical. RoboColiseum therefore modularizes the entire system with loose coupling.

### III-A Decoupled Architecture and Shared Protocol
The 'RoboColiseum Protocol' provides a standardized interface for exchanging control commands, joint states, rigid body poses, simulation timestamps, and deformed mesh geometry updates. The physics engine manages and updates the state, while rendering backends (such as Isaac Sim or OVRTX) ingest that state to render camera frames. Running in separate processes allows physics and rendering to execute asynchronously at different frame rates.

### III-B Pluggable Physics Engines
Users can switch between PhysX, Newton, and the high-accuracy contact solver libuipc depending on their needs. Engine adapters implement common conventions for initialization, step execution, and state reading, so task scripts remain agnostic to engine-specific details.

### III-C Rigid-Deformable Interactions (libuipc and IPC)
Thin-shell triangle models represent thin membranes like cloth and drawstring bags, supporting plastic bending to maintain paper creases. For soft objects like blocks, tetrahedral finite element methods (Neo-Hookean model) are used. These are solved robustly using Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), which guarantees penetration-free, stable contact forces.

### III-D Efficient Coupling of Robot Dynamics and IPC
Heavy robot articulated dynamics are stepped forward rapidly on a CPU MuJoCo worker, and the resulting robot link poses and velocities are fed kinematically into IPC as boundary conditions. Because IPC can dedicate its resources solely to deformable and contact computations, the overall computational overhead is drastically reduced.

captions.F6: System architecture diagram centered on the RoboColiseum Protocol. The control client, multiple physics adapters (PhysX/Newton/libuipc), and rendering adapters (Isaac Sim/OVRTX) connect loosely via the shared protocol, enabling modular engine swapping as needed.

sections.heading: Eight Evaluation Tracks and Budgets: Benchmarking Real Embodied AI Capabilities
sections.summary: The benchmark spans eight tracks: foundational skills like language understanding and spatial reasoning (Season I), complemented by dexterity, whole-body coordination, precision manipulation, and transferability (Season II). Action budgets and dynamic hidden test sets enforce strict rules against overfitting and brute-force shortcuts.
sections.details:
To dissect both the reasoning intellect and physical dexterity of models, the authors built an evaluation framework consisting of eight tracks.

### IV-A Season I: Four Foundational Tracks
Comprises four tracks testing basic intelligence and manipulation:
- **Instruction Following**: 10 tasks requiring the robot to identify the correct target from diverse prompts involving colors, shapes, categories, and logical negations.
- **Spatial Reasoning**: 8 tasks testing relative positions (left, right, distance) and size sorting to stack or align objects.
- **General Manipulation**: 10 tasks demanding sequential grasping, carrying, and state changes, such as bimanual pot carrying, tidying up, and scooping popcorn.
- **Robustness**: 5 disturbance categories testing stability under background lighting changes, viewpoint shifts, camera noise, and initial pose perturbations.

### IV-B Season II: Four Advanced Capability Tracks
Four newly added tracks designed to challenge higher-level physical embodiment:
- **Dexterous Manipulation**: Tasks requiring multi-fingered hands (Wuji hand) to cut with scissors, pull books from shelves, or fold cloth. These demand coordinated, independent finger control beyond simple two-finger grippers.
- **Whole-Body Coordination**: Coordinating mobile bases, torsos, and arms. Long-horizon tasks like tray serving, trash pickup, and door traversal require simultaneous navigation and pose control.
- **Precision Manipulation**: 8 tasks requiring millimeter-level alignment, such as inserting straws, capping pens, and plugging in LAN cables or chargers.
- **Cross-Embodiment Transfer**: Testing adaptation across diverse embodiments (ARX, AgileX, G1, G2) with varying kinematic structures and reach on shared tasks (opening trash cans, hanging cups, pouring liquids).

### IV-C–E Rules and Budget-Aware Scoring
The test setup uses both a fixed official set and dynamic hidden sets that regenerate with each submission to prevent memorization. Scoring incorporates action step budgets ($B_j$). Models receive progress points at checkpoints (up to 100), and a completion bonus (25 points) is awarded only if the entire task finishes within the budget. If steps exceed 1.5 times the budget, the score drops to zero, firmly ruling out policies that brute-force solutions over infinite steps.

sections.heading: 0.9686 Real-Robot Correlation and Where Modern VLAs and Agents Stand
sections.summary: Achieving a 0.9686 task score correlation across 22 real-simulation setups confirms the benchmark's reliability. Public leaderboards for Season I and Season II compare LLM agents like Claude and GPT against VLA models like π0.5, highlighting major weaknesses across models in precision and multi-fingered manipulation.
sections.details:
The paper provides thorough validation of the benchmark and detailed evaluations of current leading models.

### V-A Real2Sim Fit and Task Correlation
In 15 long-horizon tracking experiments on isolated robot arms, joint position RMSE stayed remarkably low across 21 joint/excitation conditions, ranging from 0.035 to 1.002 degrees. Furthermore, comparing task scores across 16 tasks and 22 robot configurations yielded a Pearson correlation of $r = 0.9686$ ($R^2 = 0.938$) between real hardware and simulation (Figure F8). This demonstrates that performance rankings in simulation directly reflect real-world execution.

### V-B Insights from the Season I Leaderboard
In the four foundational tracks, Prime-0 took first place with an Overall score of 77.54, leading in instruction following, general manipulation, and robustness. HiDream-O1-Embodied followed closely at 76.92, achieving the highest score on spatial reasoning. These results confirm that foundational integration of language, space, and action has reached a mature level.

### V-C & D Season II: The Wall Current Models Face
Season II evaluated eight agent systems that output robot control commands via Agent2Act alongside three supervised fine-tuned VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, LingBot-VLA-2.0, GR00T N1.7).

- **Agent Systems**: Claude Fable 5.2 led overall with 18.30, scoring high in precision manipulation (33.04) and cross-embodiment transfer (17.99). In whole-body coordination, GPT-6 Astra (18.96) and Claude Opus 5.5 (18.94) fought for top spots. However, on dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands, every agent collapsed to near-zero scores (0.00 to 5.19).
- **VLA Systems**: $\pi_{0.5}$ ranked highest with an Overall score of 11.22, leading in transfer, whole-body coordination, and dexterity. Yet in precision manipulation, every model remained stuck around 4 points, including GR00T N1.7 at 4.60.

These findings make it clear: while modern embodied models excel at coarse reasoning and navigation planning, they share severe bottlenecks when it comes to millimeter-level alignment and multi-fingered contact control.

captions.F7: Comparison scenes of basic object and deformable manipulation between the real setup (rows 1 & 3) and simulation (rows 2 & 4). Across diverse embodiments like G1, G2, and ARX X5, the real-world environments are replicated with high physical and visual fidelity.

sections.heading: Recognizing the Limits: Missing Force Feedback and the Road Ahead
sections.summary: Current limitations include a limited number of Real2Sim validation tasks and one-way coupling that lacks contact force feedback from deformables to the robot. Fully releasing evaluation logs and realizing a closed co-evolution loop—where benchmark insights feed into simulation and training data—remain future priorities.
sections.details:
While this study marks a major leap forward for simulation-based evaluation, the authors acknowledge several clear limitations.

- **Real2Sim Identification Scope**: Validation is currently restricted to 22 task setups. In addition, stiff feedback controller gains still risk masking discrepancies in hardware dynamic parameters.
- **One-Way Coupling**: While robot kinematics are passed to the deformable solver (IPC), reaction and contact forces from deformed bodies are not fed back to the MuJoCo robot simulation. Consequently, complex dynamics where heavy contact resistance pushes back on joint trajectories cannot yet be reproduced.
- **Leaderboard Transparency**: On the public leaderboard, detailed inference call counts and per-episode denominators are not fully open, limiting strict causal comparisons across different model families.

Ultimately, the paper's core vision is a co-evolution loop: using diagnosis from evaluations to refine simulators and collect targeted training data, evolving models and environments together. Demonstrating this loop quantitatively is the key next step.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Solid Foundation for the Next Embodied AI Breakthrough
sections.summary: RoboColiseum integrates rigorous system identification, a modular multi-physics setup, and an eight-track benchmark. By providing a dependable simulation testbed with high real-world correlation, it offers an essential compass for advancing future robot foundation models.
sections.details:
RoboColiseum is an innovative platform that unites system identification, decoupled physics/rendering architecture, and multidimensional capability benchmarking. As demonstrated by its 0.9686 task score correlation with real hardware, the platform proves that simulated metrics can serve as a dependable gauge of real-world performance.

Through its Season I and Season II leaderboards, the benchmark has mapped the capability profiles of leading VLA models and agent systems, exposing their stark limitations in precision alignment and multi-fingered control. By incorporating resource budgets and intermediate progress scoring, RoboColiseum provides an objective diagnostic tool that will serve as a strong catalyst for training next-generation embodied intelligence and developing advanced simulators.

takeaways: Simulator evaluation should not be judged by appearance alone, but by real-to-sim task score correlation under identical commands (demonstrating r = 0.9686 here).
Decoupling physics (rigid and deformable) from rendering via a shared protocol allows fast, modular simulation of large-scale, contact-rich manipulation.
While modern VLAs and LLM agents handle linguistic reasoning and coarse navigation well, they still face massive hurdles in millimeter precision and multi-fingered coordination.
Fair benchmark comparisons require progress-based scoring that accounts for action step and compute budgets, preventing brute-force trial and error.
limitations: Coupling is currently one-way: robot kinematics drive deformables, but reaction forces from deformed objects are not fed back to the robot dynamics solver.
Real2Sim validation covers only 22 task configurations, meaning high-gain PD controllers may still partially mask underlying model parameter errors.
Granular inference costs and raw per-episode logs for some leaderboard models have not yet been fully released to the public.
